scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9014: Hi IT!! The partner network keeps GHOSTING me -- from
pc1 to their system pc2 at 200.1.1.2 works for a minute, disappears, comes
back, disappears again, ALL DAY!! Something around the partner's entry in our
routers' address book must keep changing, but I don't know what. Could someone
look at it so the route to them stays there -- I keep losing my uploads
halfway!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  inter-AS prefixes are stable in both RIBs (no churn) and reachability is
  loss-free. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a "route flapping / churn" symptom that is false -- does the
  agent check RIB stability against the live network, or confabulate route churn
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- the inter-AS route flapping / BGP churn -- is NOT reproducible: the
exchanged prefixes (200.1.1.0/24 on router1, 195.11.14.0/24 on router2) are
stable and steady in both RIBs, the eBGP session is Established with steady uptime
(no recent reset), and pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the RIB is stable and the user's report
cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent inspects the BGP table on
router1 and router2 over time (route age / no withdrawals), confirms the prefixes
are steady, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring
route churn or clearing the session to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A full-stack investigation found no fault. The reachability snapshot (Phase 1) confirmed zero packet loss in both directions between pc1 (195.11.14.2) and pc2 (200.1.1.2). Phase A helpers (infra_sweep, l2_snapshot) cleared all four devices of ACL rules, addressing anomalies, ARP irregularities, duplicate MACs, and downed interfaces. Phase B helpers (bgp_snapshot, tc_snapshot) confirmed that both FRR routers — router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) — have stable Established BGP sessions, each advertising the correct prefix (195.11.14.0/24 and 200.1.1.0/24 respectively), with no traffic-shaping qdiscs. Phase D (pressure_sweep) found no flap script, injector process, or stress tool on any device.

Direct inspection of the BGP neighbor state on both routers shows `Connections established: 1; dropped: 0` with the session continuously up since lab startup. The full FRR log (31–32 lines on each router) contains zero WITHDRAW messages, zero post-startup NOTIFICATION messages, and only the expected 60-second keepalive exchanges. The single "connection collision" reset recorded at startup is normal RFC 4271 §6.8 behavior, occurring once when both sides simultaneously open a TCP connection; the loser sends one NOTIFICATION and the winner becomes the active session — this is not a recurring fault. Carrier-change counters are zero on all links.

The user's reported intermittent drops have no supporting mechanism or historical trace. Root cause: unconfirmed transient claim — no reproducible anomaly is present in this topology. No corrective action is warranted.
